title: Ezekiel 37:15–28
context: Ezekiel 37:15–28 is a sign-act with its explanation. The LORD tells the prophet, addressed as son of man, to take two sticks, writing on one, “For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions”, and on the other, “For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions”, and to join them into one stick in his hand (37:16–17). When the people ask what this means, he is to announce that the LORD will join Ephraim and Judah, gather the children of Israel from among the nations, and make them one nation in the land under one king (37:18–22). The division of the kingdom after Solomon (compare 1 Kings 12:19) is reversed, recalling the hope of Isaiah 11:13. The LORD promises to cleanse them from idols, so that “they will be my people, and I will be their God” (37:23), and says, “My servant David will be king over them. They all will have one shepherd.” (37:24; compare 34:23–24; Jeremiah 23:5; 30:9; Hosea 3:5). The promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:12–16 is shared ground for both traditions. Readers take this David as a future king from David’s line rather than David himself returned, and Christian readers in both traditions commonly see the promise fulfilled in Christ, the Son of David; some also expect a further fulfillment for Israel. The LORD then promises “a covenant of peace” and “an everlasting covenant”, and says he will set his sanctuary among them forever, with his tent among them (37:26–28; compare 34:25; Leviticus 26:11–12). Paul quotes this covenant language in 2 Corinthians 6:16, and Revelation 21:3 echoes it in the new creation. Readers understand the fulfillment in different ways: in the return from exile and the rebuilt community, in Christ and the church as the temple of the living God, in a future national restoration of Israel, or in some combination. Each of these readings is held within both traditions.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came again to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came again to Ezekiel. Arminian readers note that the new word follows directly after the vision of the bones, and they see the sign of the two sticks as continuing the theme of restoration from life to unity in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link and observe that the restored nation is now pictured as united. They read the verse as introducing a sign-act whose meaning will be explained, a pattern common in Ezekiel, and both traditions see it as shared ground on God’s plan to restore his people.

verses.text: “You, son of man, take one stick and write on it, ‘For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions.’ Then take another stick, and write on it, ‘For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to take two sticks and write on them for Judah and for Joseph, the stick of Ephraim. Arminian readers note that the sticks represent the southern and northern kingdoms, and they see a sign of hope that the division after Solomon would be healed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reference to the two kingdoms and compare 1 Kings 12:19, “So Israel rebelled against David’s house to this day.” They read the writing on the sticks as a vivid sign of God’s purpose to reunite his people under one rule.

verses.text: Then join them for yourself to one another into one stick, that they may become one in your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says to join the sticks into one stick in the prophet’s hand. Arminian readers note the simplicity of the sign, which ordinary people could understand, and they see in it God’s desire to heal the long division among his people and make them one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same sign and observe that how the sticks were joined is not described in detail. They read the verse as shared ground on God’s purpose of unity, and they compare Isaiah 11:13, where the envy between Ephraim and Judah departs.

verses.text: “When the children of your people speak to you, saying, ‘Won’t you show us what you mean by these?’
verses.arminianNotes: The people ask, “Won’t you show us what you mean by these?” Arminian readers note that the sign provokes the question, and they see God using visible actions to draw people into hearing his word and considering its meaning for their lives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the question gives the prophet the opportunity to explain the sign. They observe that this pattern recurs in Ezekiel’s sign-acts, and both traditions see it as an example of God’s patient teaching of a people who needed help to understand.

verses.text: tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his companions; and I will put them with it, with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they will be one in my hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will take the stick of Joseph and the stick of Judah “and make them one stick, and they will be one in my hand.” Arminian readers note the shift from the prophet’s hand to God’s hand, and they see the unity as God’s own work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same shift and read it as showing that the restoration depends on God’s power. They observe that the promise reaches beyond what the exiles could achieve, and both traditions see it as shared ground on the unity God gives to his people.

verses.text: The sticks on which you write will be in your hand before their eyes.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The sticks on which the prophet writes will be in his hand before their eyes. Arminian readers note that the sign remains visible to the people, and they see in it a reminder that God’s promises are meant to be seen, considered, and believed by those who hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same visibility and read it as confirming the certainty of God’s word. They observe that the sign-act serves as a pledge of what God will do, and both traditions treat the verse as shared ground on the role of visible signs in prophecy.

verses.text: Say to them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the nations where they have gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will take the children of Israel from among the nations, gather them, and bring them into their own land. Arminian readers note God’s faithfulness to the covenant promise of the land, and they see the gathering as a sign of his care for a scattered people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same promise and read it alongside 36:24. They observe that readers understand its fulfillment in different ways, in the return from exile, in the gathering of God’s people in Christ, or in a future restoration of Israel, and both traditions include each view.

verses.text: I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel. One king will be king to them all. They will no longer be two nations. They won’t be divided into two kingdoms any more at all.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will make them one nation on the mountains of Israel, with one king over them all, no longer two kingdoms. Arminian readers note the promise of unity and one king, and they see it as the reversal of the division that marked Israel’s history after Solomon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reversal and read the one king as preparing for the promise of David in 37:24. They observe that the unity is political and spiritual, and both traditions treat the promise as shared ground on God’s purpose to gather his people under one ruler.

verses.text: They won’t defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions; but I will save them out of all their dwelling places in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them. So they will be my people, and I will be their God.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises to cleanse them from idols and transgressions, “So they will be my people, and I will be their God.” Arminian readers note that cleansing and covenant belong together, and they see the promise as God’s gracious renewal of a people who had defiled themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link between cleansing and covenant and compare 36:25–27. They read the covenant formula as the heart of God’s promise, and both traditions treat the verse as shared ground on God’s saving and cleansing work.

verses.text: “ ‘ “My servant David will be king over them. They all will have one shepherd. They will also walk in my ordinances and observe my statutes, and do them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “My servant David will be king over them. They all will have one shepherd.” Arminian readers note the parallels in 34:23–24, Jeremiah 23:5, 30:9, and Hosea 3:5, named without harmonizing, and they read David as a future king of David’s line.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same parallels and observe that Christian readers in both traditions commonly see the promise fulfilled in Christ, the Son of David. They hold the details of fulfillment open, and they read the promise of 2 Samuel 7:12–16 as shared ground.

verses.text: They will dwell in the land that I have given to Jacob my servant, in which your fathers lived. They will dwell therein, they, and their children, and their children’s children, forever. David my servant will be their prince forever.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will dwell in the land forever, and “David my servant will be their prince forever.” Arminian readers note the emphasis on permanence, and they see the promise as pointing beyond any merely temporary restoration to a lasting rule under God’s chosen king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same emphasis and read it with 2 Samuel 7:13, “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever”, named without harmonizing. They observe that readers differ on how the land promise is fulfilled, and both traditions include several views.

verses.text: Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them. It will be an everlasting covenant with them. I will place them, multiply them, and will set my sanctuary among them forever more.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them. It will be an everlasting covenant with them.” Arminian readers note the echo of 34:25, named without harmonizing, and they see the covenant of peace as God’s gift of security and wholeness to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the everlasting covenant within the unfolding of God’s covenant purposes. They observe that the promise to set his sanctuary among them forever points to God’s abiding presence, which both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: My tent also will be with them. I will be their God, and they will be my people.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “My tent also will be with them. I will be their God, and they will be my people.” Arminian readers note the echo of Leviticus 26:11–12, named without harmonizing, and they see the promise of God’s dwelling among his people as the fulfillment of the covenant’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and observe that Paul quotes this covenant language in 2 Corinthians 6:16, “For you are a temple of the living God.” They read the promise as shared ground, with Revelation 21:3 echoing it in the new creation.

verses.text: The nations will know that I am the LORD who sanctifies Israel, when my sanctuary is among them forever more.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the nations will know that he sanctifies Israel “when my sanctuary is among them forever more.” Arminian readers note that God’s presence among his people is a witness to the nations, and they see the promise as reaching outward to all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same witness and read the sanctuary as God’s presence that sets his people apart. They observe that readers understand its fulfillment in the return, in Christ and the church, in a future restoration, or in the new creation, and both traditions include these views.
